title: The mango simile
hookLine: a man asleep under a tree, woken by a falling mango, picks it up, smells it, eats it: the steps of one perception (a commentary simile)

cards: Hot afternoon. A man lies asleep at the foot of a mango tree, his head covered with a cloth. The leaves are still.
Then a ripe mango lets go of its branch, drops, and lands with a thump right by his ear. That's the whole setup. It isn't from the suttas.

It's a simile from the commentaries, the teachers who came after and tried to make the Abhidhamma's road easy to remember. Yesterday's road was a diagram. Today it gets a body, a tree, and a piece of fruit.

teach.b: Follow the man, and you're following yesterday's road. First, sleep. His sleep is the quiet current of the mind, running along with nothing in particular in it.
The falling mango is the object striking, and the thump that wakes him is the current being cut.
Second, he wakes and turns. He pulls the cloth off his head and looks around: the mind turning toward the door the object came in by. He sees the mango: just seeing.
Third, the sorting. He picks it up: receiving. He squeezes it a little: examining.
He smells it and decides, ripe: the settling, the moment that says, this is a mango, a good one. Fourth, the eating.
He eats it, and enjoys it.

teach.h: THE EATING IS WHERE HE ACTS.
teach.b: In the simile, the eating is the response, javana, where the mind acts and kamma is made. Then he swallows the last of the taste, lies back down, and falls asleep again, until the next mango.
Notice what he chose and what he didn't. He didn't choose the mango falling, or waking, or seeing it. Most of the simile happens to him.

Only at the eating does he do something, and even then it's a very ordinary thing. That's the point the teachers wanted remembered. Life drops mangoes: sounds, sights, a message, a smell from someone's kitchen.
Most of the road is automatic. The place to look is the eating: what the mind does with what has fallen.

how: Teachers of the Abhidhamma in Theravada communities use the mango simile to explain the stages of a single perception, and some insight meditation retreats use slow, mindful eating as an exercise.

o: a teaching that pleasure is a fruit to be avoided
a commentary picture of how one perception unfolds
a sutta story about a fruit the Buddha once ate

games.q: the mango falls: tap the pairs.
p: the quiet current of the mind
the settling: this is a mango

s: the mango simile comes from one of the Buddha's discourses
it's a commentary simile, from the teachers who explained the Abhidhamma.
in the simile, the man chooses to wake up
the falling mango wakes him; most of the simile happens to him.
at the end of the simile, the man goes back to sleep
the quiet current runs on until the next mango falls.

games.q: you're the man under the tree. a ripe mango has thumped by your ear, and you've picked it up and smelled it. what happens next in the simile?
o: you climb the tree for more
games.why: he eats it and enjoys it. that's the response, javana, where the mind acts and kamma is made. then he lies back down and sleeps.

practice: If you have a piece of fruit nearby, a grape, a slice of apple, a raisin, hold it; if not, use a sip of water or tea. Look at it, feel its weight and skin, smell it, and notice when the mind says ripe, good, I want this.
Then eat it slowly, watch the liking happen, and rest in the quiet after, the way the man lies back down under his tree.

wordCard.voice: The mango simile. A commentary picture of one perception: the man asleep, the falling fruit, waking, seeing, picking up, smelling, eating, and sleep again. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: mango, the fruit and the tree.

carryVoice: Your line: the mango falls. Then back to sleep, until the next thump. Rest well.
